1903-1928

Caption This

A Clash of Cultures - The 1920s

14

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

“Does the Home You Love Love You?”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color magazine ad from Norton Ch. 22. Big words at the top ask, “Does the Home You Love Love You?” In a round picture, a smiling woman plugs a cord into a wall outlet next to a toaster and a coffee urn. Small pictures around her show a waffle iron, an electric range, a heater, an iron, and more. The ad says Westinghouse and is dated 1925.

Heads up: This ad was made to sell things. Aim your joke at the toaster, the coffee urn, the cords, or the big question in the headline. Never joke about the woman in the picture or about women’s work at home.

  • Read the big headline at the top. What is the ad asking you to think about your own home?
  • Count the appliances in the small pictures. What does the ad want you to do next?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: consumer culture
Image 2 of 5

Zelda and Scott Fitzgerald

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 22. A woman and a man stand arm in arm on stone steps beside some flowers. Norton says they are Zelda Fitzgerald and her husband, the writer F. Scott Fitzgerald, in 1926. She has short wavy hair and a scarf. He wears a light jacket, a striped shirt, and knee-length pants with tall socks.

Heads up: Real people are in this photo. Aim your joke at the stairs, the pose, or the Jazz Age party spirit. Never joke about how anyone looks, or about flappers or young women.

  • Look at how the two people stand and where they look. What mood does the photo give you?
  • Norton says Zelda was called “the First American Flapper.” What do you think a flapper was?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Jazz Ageflappers
Image 3 of 5

“Russian Ballet” (1916)

Not done

What you’re looking at: A painting from Norton Ch. 22. Bright triangles, blocks, and curves in green, pink, blue, red, and yellow overlap each other. Norton says it shows a ballet on a stage, but you have to look hard to find the dancers. The artist, Max Weber, painted it in 1916.

Heads up: Many people in the 1920s hated modern art. Aim your joke at the shapes, the colors, or how hard it is to find the dancers. Never joke about the artist or about any group of people.

  • Look for the dancers. Where are they hiding? Why would a painter break a dance into shapes?
  • Many traditional art lovers hated paintings like this. What might one of them say?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: modernismfundamentalism
Image 4 of 5

The Scopes “Monkey Trial”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 22. A packed courtroom is full of men in shirts and ties. Papers, books, and straw hats cover the tables. One man in a dark suit stands and reads from papers in his hands. A man at the right sits back in shirt sleeves and suspenders. Norton’s caption names John Scopes, Clarence Darrow, and William Jennings Bryan, and says the room was sweltering.

Heads up: This is a serious one. The trial was about real people and a deep disagreement over science and religion. Write one clear line. No jokes about anyone’s beliefs, and no jokes about the people in the photo. Look at the crowd, the papers, and the heat.

  • Look at the tables. What is piled on them? What does that tell you about a trial?
  • Norton says the heat rose above 100 degrees. What signs of the heat and the crowd do you see?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Scopes Trial (1925)fundamentalism
Image 5 of 5

The Teapot Dome cartoon

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color cartoon from Norton Ch. 22. A giant steamroller shaped like a teapot, with “OIL SCANDAL” on its side, rolls down a road and chases two frightened men. A sign points the way to “White House Highway.” Norton says the cartoon is from 1924 and shows Washington officials trying to outrun the Teapot Dome Scandal.

Heads up: This is a political cartoon about a corruption scandal. Aim your joke at the giant teapot, the steamroller, or the sign. Never joke about how the men look or about anyone who was hurt.

  • Read the red words on the teapot and the sign at the left. Where is the road headed?
  • Look at the two men. What is their mood? What are they running from?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Teapot Dome Scandal (1923)
